messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

It's been three years since his wife, Margaret, passed away after a long battle with cancer. For 69-year-old Henry, a financial analyst, the grief still feels like an open wound. He recalls the day she died as if it were yesterday - the beeping of the hospital machines, the sterile smell of the ICU, and the sound of her frail voice whispering "I love you" for the last time. These memories still linger in his mind, often popping up uninvited like a cruel joke. Whenever Henry hears about someone losing a loved one or attends funerals, he's instantly transported back to that fateful day. The pain and sadness he tries so hard to suppress come flooding back, making him feel irritable and on edge. He can't bear the thought of visiting cemeteries or talking about grief-related topics, fearing it might unravel what little composure he has left. These triggers have become a constant threat, reminding him of his vulnerability and the intense negative emotions that accompany them. To cope with these feelings, Henry has developed a set of maladaptive strategies. He numbs his emotions by throwing himself into work, spending long hours staring at spreadsheets and financial reports, trying to distract himself from the ache in his heart. When memories or thoughts about Margaret do creep up, he suppresses them quickly, not allowing himself to dwell on the pain. However, this avoidance has a paradoxical effect - it makes him even more sensitive to triggers that might remind him of her passing. The irony isn't lost on Henry; he knows his strategies are only temporary fixes, but he can't seem to break free from the cycle. His emotional numbing and thought suppression have become an integral part of his daily routine, yet they also make him more reactive to reminders of Margaret's death. A conversation about someone else's loss or a visit to a funeral home can set off a chain reaction, leaving him feeling anxious, irritable, and physically tense. As time goes on, Henry has started to notice the toll this is taking on his relationships with others. His friends and family are growing concerned about his emotional unavailability, but he feels powerless to change. He's trapped in a vicious cycle of avoidance and reactivity, unable to confront the very emotions that might set him free. Despite his best efforts to keep his grief at bay, Henry can't shake off the feeling that it's been three years too long since he last felt truly alive. The pain is still there, simmering just beneath the surface, waiting to pounce on any trigger that dares to come close. It's this suffocating sense of being stuck that has finally brought him to seek help - a desperate attempt to break free from the prison of his own making and find some semblance of peace in a world that seems to have moved on without him.
